n: John opens his Gospel by echoing Genesis 1. Before creation, Jesus already existed as “the Word” — the one through whom God speaks and acts. He was with God and was Himself divine. Latter-day Saints understand this as the premortal Jehovah.

f.g: Greek logos — speech, reason, message. Christ is God’s self-expression. JST John 1:1 reads “In the beginning was the gospel preached through the Son.”

n: John repeats for emphasis: from the very beginning, the Word was together with God the Father. The Son is distinct from the Father yet united with Him.

f.w: The same was in the beginning with God

n: Everything that exists was created through Him. Under the Father’s direction, the premortal Christ was the Creator of the earth and worlds without number.

f.w: All things were made by him

n: He is the source of all life, and that life is light for humanity — giving understanding, guidance, and hope.

f.w: the life was the light of men

n: His light shines into a dark world, and the darkness has neither understood it nor overcome it. Both meanings fit the Greek.

f.g: Greek katalambanō can mean “grasped/understood” or “overpowered/overcome.”

n: John the Baptist enters the story — a man sent by God with a mission. (The author of this Gospel is a different John, the Beloved Disciple.)

f.g: John the Baptist, the forerunner. His name means “Jehovah is gracious.”

n: John came as a witness to testify about the Light, so that everyone might believe through his testimony. Witness is a key word in this Gospel.

f.w: to bear witness of the Light

n: John was not the Light himself. Some followers of the Baptist may have exalted him too highly, so the author makes it clear.
Christ is the true Light who gives light to every person born into the world. Latter-day Saints call this the Light of Christ, given to all.
He came into the very world He made, yet the world did not recognize Him. Creation failed to know its Creator.
He came to His own covenant people, Israel, and as a whole they did not receive Him.
But everyone who did receive Him and believe in Him received power to become God’s children — not by birth but by covenant and spiritual rebirth.

f.w: power to become the sons of God

n: These are born not through human ancestry or human effort, but by God. Spiritual birth comes from Him.

f.g: Not through physical descent or lineage.

n: The heart of the Gospel: the eternal Word became a mortal man and lived among us. Eyewitnesses saw His glory — the glory of the Father’s Only Begotten Son, full of grace and truth.

f.g: Literally “pitched His tent” — recalling the tabernacle where God’s glory dwelt in Israel.

n: John the Baptist cried out: the one coming after me ranks above me, because He existed before me. Though Jesus was born after John, He was premortally first.

f.g: Ranks ahead of me, has a higher position.

n: From His fulness we all receive blessing upon blessing. Latter-day revelation adds that Christ Himself grew “from grace to grace” until He received a fulness.

f.g: Grace upon grace — one gift following another.

n: The law came through Moses, a gift that prepared Israel. Grace and truth in their fulness came through Jesus Christ, to whom the law pointed.

f.w: the law was given by Moses

n: No one has seen God the Father at any time — except, the JST adds, those who bear record of the Son. Jesus, close to the Father’s heart, has made Him known.

f.w: No man hath seen God at any time
f.g: JST John 1:19: “No man hath seen God at any time, except he hath borne record of the Son.”

f.w: in the bosom of the Father
f.g: In the closest intimacy with the Father.
Explained, revealed; Greek exēgeomai, root of “exegesis.”

n: Now John’s testimony is told. Religious authorities send priests and Levites from Jerusalem to ask John the Baptist who he is.

f.g: In John’s Gospel often means the Jewish religious authorities, not the Jewish people as a whole.
Temple assistants from the tribe of Levi.

n: John declares plainly that he is not the Messiah. Many were wondering whether he was.
Are you Elijah? No. Are you “that prophet” Moses promised? No. The JST clarifies that John denied being the Elias who would restore all things, though he was an Elias, a forerunner.

f.g: Elijah; also a title for a forerunner or restorer. Jesus did say John was the Elias who was to come.

n: Frustrated, they press him: we need an answer for those who sent us. What do you say about yourself?

f.g: They need an official report for the Jerusalem leaders.

n: He answers with Isaiah: I am a voice crying in the wilderness — prepare the Lord’s road. He sees himself as only a voice; the message is about Another.

f.w: the voice of one crying in the wilderness

f.g: Greek form of Isaiah.

n: These messengers were from the Pharisees, the strict religious party.

f.g: A movement devoted to strict observance of the law and oral traditions.

n: They ask: then why are you baptizing, if you’re not the Messiah, Elijah, or the Prophet? Baptism suggested a new beginning only a figure of authority might start.

f.g: John’s baptism treated Jews as needing to repent and enter anew, like converts.

n: John says he baptizes only with water, but someone already standing among them, unrecognized, is far greater.
He comes after John but ranks ahead of him. John says he isn’t worthy even to untie His sandal strap — a slave’s task.

f.g: Sandal strap; untying sandals was a lowly servant’s duty.

n: This took place at Bethabara on the east side of the Jordan River, where John was baptizing.

f.g: “House of the crossing” — a ford of the Jordan; some manuscripts read “Bethany beyond Jordan.”

n: The next day John sees Jesus coming and proclaims: Look, the Lamb of God who takes away the world’s sin! Every Passover lamb and temple sacrifice pointed to Him.
This is the one I spoke of, John says — the man who comes after me but ranks before me, because He existed first.
John didn’t know Him as the Messiah at first, but his baptizing was meant to reveal Him to Israel.

f.g: Revealed, made known.

n: John testifies that he saw the Spirit come down from heaven in the form of a dove and remain on Jesus. Joseph Smith taught the dove was a sign; the Holy Ghost is a personage of spirit.
God had told John that the one on whom he saw the Spirit descend and remain would be the one who baptizes with the Holy Ghost.
John has seen it and testifies: this is the Son of God.

f.g: Testified, bore witness.

f.w: this is the Son of God

n: The next day John is standing with two of his own disciples.

f.g: One is Andrew (v. 40); the unnamed other is traditionally John, the author.

n: Watching Jesus walk by, John again says: Look, the Lamb of God!

f.g: A repeated testimony that turns his own followers toward Jesus.

n: Hearing this, the two disciples leave John and follow Jesus. John’s goal was to point people to Christ, not to keep them for himself.
Jesus turns and asks: What are you seeking? They respond, “Rabbi, where are you staying?” — they want to be with Him, not just to get an answer.

f.g: Jesus’ first words in John’s Gospel — a question for every reader.
Hebrew “my great one” — a respectful title for a teacher.

n: “Come and see,” He says. They go, see where He is staying, and spend the rest of the day with Him. It was about four in the afternoon — a time the eyewitness never forgot.

f.g: About 4 p.m., counting from sunrise.

n: One of the two was Andrew, brother of Simon Peter.

f.g: Greek for “manly.” In John’s Gospel he is often bringing others to Jesus.

n: The first thing Andrew does is find his brother Simon and tell him: We have found the Messiah!

f.g: Messiah — Hebrew for “anointed one,” the same as Greek Christos.

n: Andrew brings Simon to Jesus, who looks at him and gives him a new name: Cephas, meaning “stone” — Peter in Greek. Jesus sees what Simon will become. The JST adds that Cephas means “a seer, or a stone.”

f.g: Aramaic for “rock” or “stone”; Greek Petros. JST John 1:42: “which is by interpretation, a seer, or a stone.”
Jonah; elsewhere his father is called John.

n: The next day, as He sets out for Galilee, Jesus finds Philip and says, “Follow me.”
Philip is from Bethsaida, the hometown of Andrew and Peter, on the north shore of the Sea of Galilee.

f.g: “House of fishing.”

n: Philip finds Nathanael and announces: we have found the one Moses and the prophets wrote about — Jesus of Nazareth, Joseph’s son.

f.g: “Gift of God”; often identified with Bartholomew in the other Gospels.

f.w: of whom Moses in the law, and the prophets, did write

n: Nathanael is skeptical: can anything good come from Nazareth, a small, obscure village? Philip doesn’t argue; he simply says, “Come and see.”

f.g: A small Galilean village never mentioned in the Old Testament.

n: As Nathanael approaches, Jesus says: here is a true Israelite with no deceit in him — perhaps a contrast with Jacob, the original “Israel,” known for trickery.

f.g: Deceit, craftiness.

n: Surprised, Nathanael asks how Jesus knows him. Jesus says He saw him under the fig tree before Philip called him — a place where devout Jews often studied and prayed.

f.g: A symbol of peace and a common spot for meditation and study of the law.

n: Nathanael is won over: Rabbi, You are the Son of God, the King of Israel! Encountering Christ’s knowledge of him personally brings instant testimony.

f.w: thou art the Son of God

n: Jesus replies: you believe because I said I saw you under the fig tree? You will see much greater things.
He promises they will see heaven opened and angels ascending and descending on the Son of Man — recalling Jacob’s ladder. Jesus Himself is the connection between heaven and earth.

f.g: Hebrew “Amen, amen” — “Truly, truly,” a solemn affirmation used only in John.

f.w: angels of God ascending and descending
